---
title: "`__main__.py`"
---

`main.py` is just a naming convention with no special meaning to Python, while `__main__.py` is a special filename that Python looks for when you run a **package or directory** as a program.

## `main.py`: convention only

Python treats `main.py` like any other file. People name their entry script `main.py` so readers know where to start. You could call it `app.py` or `run.py` and nothing would change.

```zsh
python main.py      # runs it like any script
```

## `__main__.py`: the entry point of a package

When you tell Python to run a *package* (a folder) instead of a file, it looks for `__main__.py` inside it and runs that file.

```
myapp/
├── __init__.py      ← runs on import (package setup)
├── __main__.py      ← runs on `python -m myapp`
└── core.py
```

```zsh
python -m myapp       # runs myapp/__main__.py
python myapp/         # also works on a directory
python myapp.zip      # and on a zip archive
```

This is why `python -m pip`, `python -m venv`, and `python -m http.server` work. Each of those packages has a `__main__.py`.

## How it connects to `if __name__ == "__main__":`

Every module has a `__name__` variable. Its value depends on how the module was loaded:

```
How the file is loaded             __name__ value
─────────────────────────────────  ─────────────────
python core.py  (run directly)     "__main__"
import core     (imported)         "core"
python -m myapp → __main__.py      "__main__"
```

That's why this guard lets one file work both as a library and as a script:

```python
# core.py
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name}"

if __name__ == "__main__":     # only true when run directly
    print(greet("LB"))
```

A typical clean `__main__.py` stays thin and delegates to the real code:

```python
# myapp/__main__.py
from myapp.cli import main

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```
